April 16, 1917. 
Mr. Henry Fox may be reinstated as assistant engineer at $2,400 per annum in the Engineer Department at large, Little Rock, Ark., without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Fox served about 14 years under the Engineer Department at large in various 
responsible positions and was furloughed on August 31, 1909. He has since been engaged in important engineer work in connection with rivers, harbors, and canals. In addition to his large experience in river and harbor work, he has passed several high-grade examinations for responsible positions in the classified service. His services are urgently required in connection with the completion of the survey of the Arkansas River, a difficult work and one which can not be satisfactorily performed except by a person having broad experience. nl Service Commission joins with the Secretary of War in recommending this order. 
April 18, 1917. 
Mr. D. Brockman Winfrey may be appointed a clerk in the competitive classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Winfrey has been serving in the excepted position of private secretary to the Director of the Mint since November 11, 1915, and that on account of his thoroug knowledge of the general work of the Bureau of the Mint and the efficient manner 
in which he has performed his duties, it is believed that his permanent appointment will be in the interest of the service. 
May 7, 1917. 
Mrs. Annie Eopolucci may be appointed to a position as seamstress at the Wash- ington Navy Yard, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Eopolucci is the mother of John I. Eopolucci, formerly an enlisted man in the Navy, who was detailed as a gunner on the Aztec, and was the first person in the naval service of the United States to lose his life as the result of the sinking of an armed merchantman. 
May 7, 1917. : 
The appointment of Mr. Edgar Mabie as superintendent of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department is hereby authorized without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Mabie has had 14 years’ experience in one of the large insurance com- panies in New York City, passing on applications for insurance, examining policies, and having supervision of general office detail, and in view of the technical character of the work in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance, for which Jedially trained assistants are required, it is believed his appointment will be greatly in the interests of the service. 
May 8, 1917. 
‘William A. West may be appointed to the position of skilled laborer in the equip- ment shops, Post Office Department, without regard to civil-service rules and regu- lations.” ; The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of the above order. 
May 9, 1917. 
Mr. Horace M. Albright may be appointed as Assistant Director of the National - Park Service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior who states that Mr. Albright, as assistant attorney of the department, has been assisting in the management of the national park system for several years; that he is very familiar with the administration of the parks and with their problems; that he is personally acquainted with the field force and with the park concessioners who are 
under contract with the department to provide hotel accommodations and transporta-

May 9, 1917. 
Henry S. Grogan, of Minnesota, may be reinstated as a post-office inspector without regard to the year limitation prescribed by Civil Service Rule IX. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Grogan’s long and efficient service in various branches of the Postal Service, including 11 years as a letter carrier and subsequent service from 1906 to 1912 as posto-flice inspector, superintendent of station, and assistant superintendent of mails. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General for an Executive order. 
June 12, 1917. 
Mrs. E. Anna Draper and Mrs. Katherine Gaines may be appointed as clerks in the Treasury Department for service in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance, without regard to civil-service requirements. Schedule A, Subdivision VIII, paragraph 2 of the civil-service rules, making excep- tions from the requirement of examination in the Interior Department, is amended to read as follows: 
2. Inspectors whose duties are of a confidential nature in the office of the Secretary of the Interior and who are appropriated for by the Congress. 
This amendment is made for the reason that the number of employees of the sort under consideration varies from time to time by reason of changes in appropriations, and that the paragraph excepting one special land inspector and four special inspectors as heretofore does not provide for such changes. The duties devolving upon these inspectors require exceptional and unusual qualifications. he amendment is in accordance with the views of the Secretary of the Interior and the Civil Service Commission.

130 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
August 6, 1913. 
Mr. Thomas H. Vanderford may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Internal Revenue Service without reference to the period of his separation from the service. 
Mr. Vanderford was a deputy collector of internal revenue from October 11, 1893, to July 10, 1898, when he was removed for political reasons. A former collector of internal revenue, under whom he served and by whom he was separated from the service, makes the following statement regarding him in a letter dated May 9, 1913: “Mr. Vanderford was an officer in the service when I was appointed collector in 
1898 and had been for four years prior to my appointment. He served under me for practically a year. I regarded him as one of the best officers in the service and after 10 years’ experience as collector I think I can truthfully say he was as good an officer as I ever knew. I separated him from the service in order to appoint a man of my own party.” The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in a letter dated July 7, 1913, states that he has personally “known Mr. Vanderford for many years, that he is a man of sterling integrity, honest and fearless, and in his opinion possesses just such traits of character as would make a competent and efficient revenue officer. The records of the Internal Bevoune Bureau show that he rendered satisfactory service and was an efficient employee. 
In view of the above facts the commission concurs with the recommendation of the Sag of the Treasury and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the issuance of this order. 
August 9, 1913. 
Miss Sarah A. Prender, who is now serving as a skilled laborer in the Post Office Department, may be appointed to a clerical position not higher than class E on the permanent roll of that department without regard to the civil-service act. 
August 20, 1913. 
Mr. Charles M. McCabe may be reinstated as a clerk in the Postal Service without reference to the year limitation of the reinstatement rule. Mr. McCabe was removed from the Nashville, Tenn., post, office on September 10, 1898, notice of his removal alleging ‘‘inefficiency.”” No charge of inefficiency had been preferred against him and he was allowed no opportunity to reply to the charge as required by the rules then in effect. Mr. McCabe as a member of the board of civil service examiners for the Nashville post office rendered assistance to the commission in connection with investigations involving the collector of internal revenue, who was removed by the President for violation of the civil service rules. The Postmaster General states that it appears that Mr. McCabe was removed on political grounds, and the issuance of an Executive order for his reinstaterient seems to be justified by the facts in the case. In view of the facts stated above the Civil Service Commission concurs in recom- mending this order. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the appointment of Pedro Abrain to the position of 
general helper at $2.32 per diem at the navy yard, Mare Island, Cal. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Abrain was injured in the line of duty as a fireman on board the U. S. 8. Prometheus and is unable to perform the duties of a fireman. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the Sppeinishens of Edmond Pawellik to the position 
of general helper at $1.76 per diem at the navy yard, Norfolk, Va. This order 1s issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Pawellik was discharged from the Navy owing to injuries received in the line of duty and is unable to obtain civil employment.

September 11, 1913. 
Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
September 17, 1913. 
Miss Emily W. Matter, of the District of Columbia, now temporarily employed in 
the same position through certification by the Civil Service Commission, may be appointed permanently to the position of clerk at $720 per annum in the Coast and 
Geodetic Survey. : The department in recommending this action stated that Miss Matter had demon- strated her fitness during temporary appointment, that the department had been 
unable to make selection from six certifications because of declinations and of the fact that many of the eligibles were found unsuitable. 
September 17, 1913. 
Mrs. Annie S. Renick, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Green may be reinstated as a compositor in the Weather Bureau without reference to the time limit imposed by the civil-service rules. 
Mr. Green’s services as a compositor were terminated on December 31, 1910, after more than 20 years’ service. The reason given at the time was that a reduction of the force was necessary because of the transfer of certain work from the Weather Bureau to the Government Printing Office. The Secretary of Agriculture with the concur- rence of the Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement because there is reason to believe that Mr. Green was unfairly dealt with because of certain testimony he had given in a case which resulted in the reprimand of the Chief of the Weather Bureau. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. David A. Robbins, formerly a letter carrier at Boston, Mass., may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service.

NEWSPAPER READERS AND TRANSLATORS, 
October 25, 1917. 
Newspaper readers and translators selected by the Postmaster General for 
filling certain confidential positions under the trading-with-the-enemy act may

qualifications required. 
FOOD AND FUEL ADMINISTRATIONS. 
November 10, 1917. 
In view of the fact that the Food Administration and the Fuel Administration 
are created to exist only during the present war with Germany, and that the 
temporary nature and the peculiarities of the work render it difficult and some￾times impossible to obtain from the competitive classified service of the United

due to the war, such eligibles are often obtained only after delays which inter￾fere with work of an urgent nature, these administrations are authorized to

responsible charge are best adapted to the work, it being understood that all possible use will be made of the Civil Service Commission and that this order

Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. The above order was issued on request of the Postmaster General, who stated that these men were highly desirable as messengers, entirely trustworthy, and had rendered excellent service, having been directly connected with the office of the Postmaster General since the beginning of the present administration. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mr. Charles W. G. Brett may be transferred from the position of mechanician at 
$1,200 per annum to a clerkship at the same salary, in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Brett was appointed as mechanician on September 16, 1908. On March 19, 1912, he met with an accident, in the line of duty, which resulted in the loss of his left eye. His transfer to the clerical rollisrecommended by the Director of the Census, who states that Mr. Brett’s experience in connection with the various machines used in the bureau, his familiarity with the matter to be tabulated, and his general educa- tion are believed to be such as to fit him for clerical duties, and that his services have always been satisfactory. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
April 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Lillian B. S. Grant may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of time she has been sep- arated from the service. Silcott, was appointed to the position of printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Printing and Engraving on August 2, 1895, and was pro- moted to operative and through the several grades of that position. On July 1, 1902, she was transferred to the Post Office Department as clerk at $900, and was promoted to $1,000 July 1, 1905. She resigned May 9, 1912. 
The Postmaster General advises that it is stated that Mrs. Grant’s husband is a ermanent invalid, and that she is therefore compelled to provide a livelihood for Poth her husband and herself. SPECIAL RULE.
February 11, 1903.
The following special rule was promulgated:
The temporary clerks employed at the various naval stations in the insular posses¬
sions of the United States (except San Juan and Honolulu) whose names are on a
list heretofore furnished the Civil Service Commission by the Secretary of the Navy
may he absolutely appointed, it appearing that their original appointments without
examination were necessary for sufficient reasons, among which were (1) inability of
the Commission to certify eligibles who would accept promptly, (2) inability of the
Department to secure accommodations on transports, and (3) delays caused by the
failure of eligibles to accept appointment.
The effect of this rule was to bring into the classified service certain clerks who
were employed at the naval stations at Cavite, P. I.; Guam, L. I.; Honolulu, Hawaii;
Tutuila, Samoa, and San Juan, P. R. It appears that the majority of these
clerks were appointed wffien the Commission was unable to certify eligibles who
would accept promptly. There were 35 names on the list submitted by the Navy
Department and referred to in the rule of persons to be affected. Twenty-three of
these were residing at the places of their employment at the time they were
appointed and 12 were obtained in the United States.
In view of the experience gained by these persons in their several years’ service,
the disadvantage to the service of replacing them with other clerks and the fact that
their classification was in accord with the spirit of the action of Congress in placing
in the classified service clerks with somewhat the same status in the War Depart¬
ment at Washington and with the spirit of the action of the President in the case of
temporary clerks under the War Department who served in Cuba, their inclusion in
the classified service was recommended to the President for his approval.
AMENDMENT.
February 19, 1903.
Section 1 of Rule V was amended by omitting therefrofn the proviso, which pro¬
viso so omitted reads as follows:
Provided, That in order to secure a sufficient number of eligibles to meet the needs
of the service, foreign-born persons who have declared their intention to become
citizens of the United States may be admitted to examinations for the position of
copperplate map engraver.
This proviso was added to the rule by amendment on June 28, 1902, for the reason
that the Commission had repeatedly failed to secure a sufficient number of qualified
persons for the position of copperplate map engraver who were citizens of the United
States, and it was understood that qualified persons might be obtained from England,
Scotland, and Germany, where there are a number of private establishments employ¬
ing engravers of the kind desired.
It was found, however, that the change in the rule wras not essential, and the
repeal of the amendment of June 28, 1902, was therefore recommended.
REVISION OF THE RULES.«
March 20, 1903.
The President approved a revision of the civil-service rules to take effect on and
after April 15, 1903, in lieu of those promulgated on May 6, 1896, and the amend¬
ments thereof.

Mr. G. M. Davison may be reinstated as storekeeper-gauger in the Internal-Revenue Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Davison was storekeeper-gauger for several years, his final separation from that service having occurred by resignation on July 5, 1893. He is eligible for reinstatement under the rules in any of these departments because of his former service therein; but not in the Government Printing Office. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Public Printer, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, as there are no eligible applicants among the veterans employed in the Government Printing Office. October 4, 1912. 
Mr. John XK. Robinson may be reinstated as a printer in the Weather Bureau with- out reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Robinson was an enlisted man and noncommissioned officer of the Signal Corps of the Army for a number of years, and when the meteorological division of the Signal Corps became a part of the Weather Bureau he was transferred to the Weather Bureau and remained for several years, when he was discharged on false charges without proper opportunity to defend himself. 
The Acting Secretary of Agriculture and the Civil Service Commission recommend the reinstatement.

UNDER EXECUTIVE ORDER OF DECEMBER 1, 1910. 
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE. 
Dr. Frank J. Loomis as veterinary inspector. (Minute 1, July 24, 1912.) 
Dr. Loomis was appointed as a veterinary inspector at Watertown, N. Y., to be paid at the rate of $5 per diem when actually employed, not to exceed $300 per annum, under Schedule A of the civil service rules. He passed the veterinary inspector examination and was certified and offered appointment, but declined. The depart- ment desired to readjust the quarantine work along the Canadian boundary and to extend Dr. Loomis’s territory to cover Ogdensburg, N. Y., which would require a greater number of days’ employment. Authority was requested to increase his com- pensation not to exceed $800 in any fiscal year. It was claimed that the work was of such an intermittent nature that it would not justify the appointment of a regular inspector and that Dr. Loomis was a practicing veterinarian at Watertown, N. Y., I could handle the work without detriment to his private practice.

A. Lincoln Dryden as navigation officer, at $1,200 per annum. (Minute 1, May 17,

It is hereby ordered that Henry J. Cantey, a laborer in the unclassified service, at a salary of $660 per annum, in the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor, may be promoted to the position of assistant messenger in the classified service, in the same bureau, at a salary of $720 per annum, without reference to civil-service rules. It is stated by administrative officials of the Department of Labor that Mr. Cantey possesses qualifications of unusual value in the work of the Bureau of Labor Statistics. He has been with the Bureau of Labor Statistics nearly 10 years, during all of which time his record has been excellent.
